passage:
You want to know why I stopped talking at dinner, Santosh? Okay. I'm Gautam. I once said the maths tuition was too much, and my mother said, "Do you know there are children who don't have a school to go to? Be grateful." And she kept going. Every complaint got answered with somebody who had less.
I sat there feeling like garbage, guilty for being tired, and honestly angry too, because my day was still my day. I stopped complaining. That didn't make me grateful. It made me quiet.
Last month my aunt said, "It's a lot, isn't it? And you also have some lucky things." Both could be true. That was the first time I actually felt thankful, and I told her so.

qa.q: What did Gautam's mother say when Gautam said the tuition was too much?
qa.a: She said there are children who don't have a school to go to, and told Gautam to be grateful.

qa.q: How did Gautam feel while being told to be grateful?
qa.a: Guilty for being tired and angry too, because the day still felt real. Gautam felt like garbage.

qa.q: What did the aunt say that changed things for Gautam?
qa.a: She said it is a lot and that Gautam also has some lucky things, letting both be true, and then Gautam felt thankful and said so.

qa.q: How might Gautam's mother see her own words?
qa.a: She may think she is teaching thankfulness, without noticing that each complaint is answered with someone who has less, which shuts Gautam down.

grounding: A teenager told to be grateful by comparison with poorer children feels guilt and resentment and stops speaking honestly.

passage:
I'm Mehak, and I sit behind Dolma in class. Last Tuesday Dolma was close to tears over a low mark, and our teacher said, "Some children would give anything to be in this school. Be grateful." Dolma went quiet and sat very straight.
At lunch she pushed her food around and said, "Now I feel bad for being sad." I don't know exactly what was in her head, but I noticed she stopped telling anyone when she was upset.
Later I sat next to her and said, "You can be sad about the mark and still be glad to be here." Her shoulders came down a little. I think she just needed both to be allowed.

qa.q: What did the teacher say to Dolma about the low mark?
qa.a: That some children would give anything to be in this school, and to be grateful.

qa.q: What was Dolma feeling at lunch?
qa.a: Guilty for being sad, and unhappy. She pushed her food around and said she felt bad for being sad.

qa.q: What did Mehak say that helped, and why?
qa.a: Mehak said Dolma can be sad about the mark and still be glad to be here. That let both feelings be allowed, so Dolma's shoulders came down.

qa.q: What might the teacher have hoped for by saying it?
qa.a: Probably to give perspective or comfort, but it shut Dolma's feelings down instead.

grounding: A teenager told to be grateful by comparison feels guilt and shuts down, seen by a classmate.

passage:
Jyoti, can I tell you something that'll sound terrible? Yesterday I told Papa I was really stressed about the maths olympiad and didn't want to go. He said, "You should be grateful. There are children in the slum across the road who don't even have books."
And I know. I do know. But after that I felt so guilty for being stressed that I just shut up. And then I felt angry, because now I'm not allowed to feel bad about anything, ever, since someone somewhere has it worse. So I went to my room and didn't say a word at dinner.
I am grateful, mostly. I just wanted him to ask why I was scared. I'm Francis, and I think I'll stop telling him things for a while, which is the opposite of what he'd want.

qa.q: What did Papa say about the children across the road?
qa.a: That there are children in the slum across the road who don't even have books.

qa.q: What did Francis feel after being told to be grateful?
qa.a: Francis felt guilty for being stressed, then angry and resentful, as if never allowed to feel bad.

qa.q: What could Papa say instead next time?
qa.a: He could ask why Francis is scared of the olympiad and listen first, before any comparisons.

qa.q: What might Papa have been hoping for with his comment?
qa.a: Papa probably hoped to give some perspective and ease the stress, not realising it would shut down honest talk.

grounding: Shows a teenager told to be grateful by comparison with poorer children, feeling guilt and resentment and going quiet.

passage:
Monday. In the hostel common room, Anjali grumbled to the warden, Imran Sir, that dinner was cold again. He frowned. "You should be grateful you get three meals. Many children in this state don't." Anjali's face burned. She said nothing more.
Wednesday. Anjali stopped mentioning anything to Imran Sir: not the broken tap, not the leak in the roof above her bed. She felt guilty for complaining at all, and quietly annoyed that she felt guilty.
Friday. A storm soaked her mattress. Imran Sir found out only from another student. He came to her room and said, "I think I made it hard for you to tell me things. I'm sorry. Tell me what's wrong, and I'll listen first." Anjali looked at him for a long moment, then pointed at the ceiling.

qa.q: What happened to Anjali's mattress on Friday?
qa.a: A storm soaked it.

qa.q: How did Anjali feel on Wednesday?
qa.a: Anjali felt guilty for complaining at all and quietly annoyed about that guilt, so she stopped telling Imran Sir anything.

qa.q: What did Imran Sir do on Friday that repaired things?
qa.a: He admitted he had made it hard to speak, apologised, and promised to listen first.

qa.q: How did Imran Sir's Monday comment affect the hostel's problems?
qa.a: It silenced Anjali, so the broken tap and the leaking roof went unreported until the mattress was soaked.

grounding: Shows a teenager told to be grateful when she complains, and the guilt and resentment shutting down honest talk.

passage:
Kashish, you're scowling because your mother told you to be grateful? Come, sit with your Sudha Nani. When I was fourteen, I cried because I didn't get new chappals for Diwali. My father said, "Think of the children in the fields with no chappals at all." I stopped crying. I also stopped telling him anything that hurt me, for years.
I felt so guilty, and under the guilt I was angry, because the chappals weren't really the point. My friends had laughed at my old ones. That was what I wanted to tell him.
When your mother was your age, I tried to remember that. When she complained, I asked first, "What happened?" Usually there was a story underneath. So tell me. What happened?

qa.q: What did Sudha want for Diwali at fourteen?
qa.a: New chappals.

qa.q: How did young Sudha feel after her father's words?
qa.a: Sudha felt guilty and, underneath, angry, because the real hurt, friends laughing at her old chappals, went unheard.

qa.q: Which choice in the story changed how Sudha raised Kashish's mother?
qa.a: Remembering her own silence, Sudha chose to ask "What happened?" first whenever her daughter complained.

qa.q: What might Sudha's father have intended?
qa.a: He probably meant to teach gratitude, not realising it stopped Sudha from sharing what really hurt.

grounding: Shows a teenager told to be grateful by comparison with poorer children, feeling guilt and resentment and going silent.

passage:
It was exam week, the power had gone out again, and Tenzin, fifteen, was trying to study by torchlight in the small room he shared with his two younger brothers, who were fighting over a blanket.
"Ma, I can't study like this. I need my own corner. Just a table."
Sangeeta didn't look up from the stove. "Be grateful you even have a room. Children in the slums study under streetlights. You should be thankful."
Tenzin's face went hot. He did feel lucky, sometimes. Now he just felt guilty for asking, and angry that he couldn't ask.
"I wasn't complaining about my life. I just wanted—"
"Enough. Be thankful."
He went back to the torch. He didn't mention the table again. That week he didn't tell her about the chemistry test he'd done badly on, or anything else.
Later, Sangeeta noticed how quiet he had become, and wondered why.

qa.q: Who did Tenzin share his room with?
qa.a: He shared it with his two younger brothers.

qa.q: What was Tenzin feeling after Sangeeta's reply?
qa.a: Tenzin felt guilty for asking and resentful that he wasn't allowed to ask, even though he sometimes did feel lucky.

qa.q: What could Sangeeta have said instead?
qa.a: She could have listened first and said something like, "It is hard to study here. Let's see if we can find you a corner," before anything about gratitude.

qa.q: How was Sangeeta affected by the way she answered?
qa.a: Sangeeta was left puzzled and a little worried, noticing Tenzin had grown quiet without realising her words had shut down honest talk.

grounding: A teenager told to be grateful compared to poorer children feels guilt and resentment, and stops talking honestly.
